title: Indicator Removal: Clear Persistence
summary: Clear Persistence is the removal of the mechanisms and artefacts an intruder installed to keep access, performed so that investigators cannot describe how the foothold worked. The behaviour mirrors the persistence it destroys: services or daemons are stopped and deleted, scheduled tasks are unregistered, registry keys and values that carried a run key or a malicious service entry are cleaned out, launch agents and property list files on macOS are removed, systemd units and cron entries on Linux are dropped, and user or service accounts created earlier are deleted. Security operations should not read this deletion as a benign change, because it is usually a late-stage action by someone who already knows the environment, and it is often a sign of a pending exit or of a switch to a newer implant, where the old loader is removed to avoid conflicts and to reduce the number of artefacts on disk. Detection depends on comparing the current state with historical records rather than on spotting the removal live. Configuration baselines, service and task inventory snapshots, account creation and deletion events, registry and property list monitoring with a security configuration agent, and archived audit logs of the original creation all allow the analyst to reconstruct a mechanism that is no longer present, and a creation event followed days later by a matching deletion event from an unexpected account is the clearest signature.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker removes the things they installed to keep access to a system. Examples are a service, a scheduled task, a registry entry, or a fake user account. The goal is to leave no proof of how they kept coming back.
beginner.whyItMatters: Persistence items are the written record of an intrusion. They show how the attacker survived reboots and password changes. If those items are cleaned away, you may find no clear answer to how they got back in. You may also miss another foothold they left on purpose.
howItWorks: The attacker first sets up a way to stay on the system, such as a service or a scheduled task.
They may add a new user account or change a registry entry to make access easier next time.
Later, for example when they replace their tool with a newer version, the old entry point becomes a problem.
They stop and delete the service, unregister the task, and remove the registry entries they added.
They also remove any configuration files or launch items that pointed at their payload.
Finally they delete the accounts they created, so nothing suggests they could return.
beginner.example: Imagine someone hides a spare key under a flowerpot so they can enter the building another day. When they no longer want that key, they take it away and refill the pot with fresh soil. The door and the wall look normal, and only the gardener notices the soil was disturbed.
takeaways: Removing a persistence mechanism destroys proof of how access was kept, not the access itself.
The malware may have run without ever creating a file, so look for behaviour, not only files.
Compare today's services, tasks, and accounts with older inventory records to find the gap.

objectives: Explain what persistence means and why attackers remove it later.
List common persistence artefacts on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
Describe how service, task, registry, and account changes can be monitored.
Explain how baselines and inventory snapshots reveal removed persistence.
Recognise the pattern of a creation event followed by a matching deletion event.
